module_title: Splitting the Carcass and Primary Cutting

lessons.title: Splitting the carcass along the spine with a saw
lessons.body: After the pig has been bled, scalded, and scraped, and the internal organs removed, you are left with a whole carcass. To make handling easier and to begin primary cutting, you must split the carcass along the spine into two halves. This is done using a meat saw, also called a butcher's saw. A clean, sharp saw is essential. You will also need a sturdy table or hanging rail at about waist height. If you don't have a rail, lay the carcass on a clean, washed table. Position the carcass on its back or side, depending on your setup. Start at the tail end and saw through the pelvic bone, then continue up along the spine. Use long, steady strokes, letting the saw do the work. Do not force it; forcing can cause the saw to jump and injure you. As you cut, you will feel the resistance of the backbone. Keep the saw aligned with the centre of the spine. If you have a helper, one person can hold the carcass steady while the other saws. For a typical market-weight pig of 80â100 kg, splitting takes about 5â10 minutes with a good saw. Once you reach the neck, the two halves will separate. If you plan to remove the head, do that before splitting or after, but many butchers remove the head first to reduce weight. After splitting, you have two sides (halves). Wipe the cut surfaces with a clean cloth to remove bone dust. Bone dust can spoil the meat's appearance and taste, so wipe it away. Now the halves are ready for further cutting into quarters or primals. Always work on a clean surface and wash your hands and tools with soap and hot water before and after. In many African settings, this step is done outdoors on a wooden table or a clean tarp. Ensure the area is free of dust and flies. If you are not processing immediately, move the halves to a cool room or refrigerator.

lessons.title: Halving and quartering for easier handling
lessons.body: Once the carcass is split into two sides, each side is still heavy and awkward to manage. Halving and quartering make the meat easier to handle, chill, and cut into primal cuts. A side from a 90 kg pig weighs about 45 kg. That is too heavy for one person to lift comfortably. You can further divide each side into two quarters: a forequarter (front) and a hindquarter (rear). The split between fore and hind is usually made between the 5th and 6th rib, or just behind the shoulder. To quarter, lay a side on a clean table. Using a sharp knife or a saw, cut through the ribs and spine at the chosen point. For a forequarter, you will cut through the shoulder area. For a hindquarter, you cut through the loin and belly. The exact cut point can vary, but a common method is to cut at the last rib. This gives a forequarter with the shoulder, belly, and some loin, and a hindquarter with the ham, loin, and belly. After cutting, you will have four pieces: two forequarters and two hindquarters. Each quarter weighs roughly 20â25 kg, which one person can lift. Quartering also helps with chilling because smaller pieces cool faster. In hot African climates, rapid chilling is critical to prevent spoilage. If you don't have a chiller, quartering allows you to salt or smoke pieces more evenly. Use a clean saw or knife, and wipe the cut surfaces. Keep your tools sharp; a dull knife tears meat and creates a poor appearance. Always cut on a stable surface. If you are selling at a market, quartering allows you to display and price different sections. For example, a hindquarter with the ham may fetch a higher price per kg than a forequarter. Record the weight of each quarter if you are tracking yields. After quartering, move the pieces to a cool place or continue cutting into primal cuts.

lessons.title: Identifying primal cuts: shoulder, loin, belly, and ham
lessons.body: After quartering, you will break each quarter into primal cuts. The four main primal cuts of a pig are the shoulder, loin, belly, and ham. Knowing these cuts helps you price and sell meat according to local demand. Start with the shoulder. The shoulder is the front leg and adjacent area. It includes the picnic shoulder (lower part) and the Boston butt (upper part). Shoulder meat is well-marbled, flavourful, and often used for stews, mince, or roasting. In many African markets, shoulder is sold as bone-in or boneless chunks. Next, the loin. The loin runs along the back from the shoulder to the ham. It includes the rib end, centre loin, and sirloin. The loin is the source of chops, roasts, and back bacon. It is lean and tender. To identify the loin, look for the eye muscle along the spine. The belly is the underside of the pig, from the shoulder to the ham. It is fatty and used for bacon, pork belly, and lard. In African cooking, belly is often cut into strips for grilling or frying. Finally, the ham is the rear leg. It is the largest primal and is used for fresh roasts, curing, or making ham. The ham includes the leg and rump. To separate these cuts, you will use a knife and saw. For example, to remove the ham from the loin, cut through the spine at the hip joint. To separate the shoulder from the loin, cut between the 4th and 5th rib. Each primal can be further processed. For a 90 kg pig, typical yields are: shoulder about 20%, loin about 20%, belly about 15%, ham about 25%, and other parts (head, feet, offal) about 20%. Knowing these percentages helps you estimate how much meat you will have for sale. Always cut on a clean surface and keep your knives sharp. Label each primal if you are storing them.

lessons.title: Removing the head and preparing it for local dishes
lessons.body: The head of the pig is often removed before or after splitting the carcass. Removing the head reduces the weight of the carcass and provides valuable meat for local dishes. To remove the head, you will need a sharp knife and a meat saw. First, position the carcass on its back or side. Locate the joint between the skull and the first neck vertebra (atlas joint). Cut through the skin and flesh around the neck, then use the saw to cut through the bone at the joint. Twist the head to separate it. For a 90 kg pig, the head weighs about 5â7 kg. After removal, you can further process the head. Many African cultures use pig head for dishes like head cheese, stews, or soups. The cheeks, tongue, and brain are considered delicacies. To prepare, first singe any remaining hair with a blowtorch or over an open flame. Then wash the head thoroughly with warm water and scrub with a brush. You can split the head in half using a saw or cleaver to access the brain and tongue. Remove the tongue and set aside. The brain can be scooped out and used for dishes like scrambled eggs with brain or fried brain. The cheeks are often cured or cooked slowly. In West Africa, pig head is used in pepper soup; in Southern Africa, it may be boiled and served with pap. Ensure you clean the head well to remove any dirt or blood. Soak it in salt water for 30 minutes if desired. Then cook according to your recipe. If you are not using the head immediately, refrigerate or freeze it. The head should be chilled quickly to prevent spoilage. Always wash your hands and tools after handling raw meat. Properly prepared, the head adds value and reduces waste.

lessons.title: Chilling the carcass to firm up the meat
lessons.body: Chilling is a critical step after slaughter and cutting. It firms up the meat, making it easier to cut and improving its texture and shelf life. In hot African climates, meat can spoil within hours if not chilled. Ideally, the carcass should be chilled to below 4Â°C as quickly as possible. If you have a walk-in chiller or refrigerator, place the halves or quarters on clean trays or hooks. Ensure there is space between pieces for air circulation. Do not stack meat; stacking slows cooling and can cause spoilage. If you don't have refrigeration, you can use alternative methods. One method is to hang the carcass in a cool, well-ventilated shed and use a fan to circulate air. You can also pack the meat in ice in a clean cooler box. For a 90 kg pig, you will need about 20â30 kg of ice. Place a layer of ice at the bottom of the cooler, then a layer of meat, then more ice, and so on. Keep the cooler in the shade. Another method is to use a evaporative cooler (zeer pot) for smaller pieces. Chilling the carcass for 12â24 hours is ideal. This allows rigor mortis to resolve, making the meat more tender. After chilling, the meat will be firm and easier to saw into chops or cuts. If you are selling fresh meat, chilling also improves appearance. Never leave meat at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Bacteria multiply rapidly above 4Â°C. Use a thermometer to check the temperature if possible. After chilling, you can proceed to weigh and package the meat. Remember to maintain hygiene: wash hands, clean surfaces, and keep insects away. In many African markets, meat is sold fresh, but chilling is still important for quality.

lessons.title: Weighing and recording yields for pricing
lessons.body: Weighing and recording yields is essential for pricing your pork accurately and for managing your business. After chilling, weigh each primal cut and any other parts (head, feet, offal). Use a reliable scale, preferably a digital hanging scale or platform scale. For a 90 kg live pig, the dressed carcass weight (after removing head, organs, and blood) is typically about 70â75% of live weight, so around 63â68 kg. After splitting and quartering, you will have various cuts. Weigh each cut separately. For example, a hindquarter might weigh 15â18 kg, a forequarter 12â15 kg, loin 8â10 kg, belly 6â8 kg, and shoulder 10â12 kg. Record these weights in a notebook or a simple spreadsheet. Also record the weight of the head, feet, and offal. This data helps you calculate your yield percentage. For example, if you sell the loin for 50 units per kg, you can calculate expected revenue. Pricing should cover your costs: feed, labour, slaughter, and overheads. In many African markets, pork is sold per kg, but sometimes per piece. Knowing the weight of each cut allows you to set a fair price. For example, if the total cost of raising the pig was 500 units, and you have 65 kg of saleable meat, your cost per kg is about 7.7 units. You then add your profit margin. Record sales as well, so you know which cuts sell best. This helps you plan future pig production. Always keep records for at least a year. Use a simple book or a mobile app. If you are selling at a market, a small notebook is fine. Accurate records also help you compare yields from different pigs or feeds. Over time, you can improve efficiency. Finally, ensure your scale is calibrated and clean. Weigh meat on a clean tray or paper. After weighing, package and label the meat with weight and price. This builds trust with customers.

quiz.q: What tool is primarily used to split the carcass along the spine?
quiz.explanation: A meat saw is designed for cutting through bone and splitting the carcass.

quiz.q: Why should you wipe the cut surfaces after splitting the carcass?
quiz.explanation: Bone dust from sawing can spoil the appearance and taste of the meat, so it should be wiped away.

quiz.q: At what weight does a side from a 90 kg pig typically come in?
quiz.explanation: A 90 kg pig yields two sides of about 45 kg each.

quiz.q: Where is the split between forequarter and hindquarter usually made?
quiz.explanation: The common cut point for quartering is between the 5th and 6th rib.

quiz.q: What is one benefit of quartering the carcass?
options: A) Easier handling and faster chilling
quiz.explanation: Quartering makes pieces lighter and allows faster cooling, which is important in hot climates.

quiz.q: Which primal cut includes the front leg and adjacent area?
quiz.explanation: The shoulder primal is the front leg and surrounding meat.

quiz.q: What is the belly primarily used for?
quiz.explanation: The belly is fatty and commonly used for bacon, pork belly, and lard.

quiz.q: Which primal cut is the largest?
quiz.explanation: The ham is the rear leg and is typically the largest primal cut.

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of a 90 kg pig is the ham?
quiz.explanation: The ham typically accounts for about 25% of the carcass weight.

quiz.q: How much does the head of a 90 kg pig typically weigh?
quiz.explanation: The head of a market-weight pig weighs around 5â7 kg.

quiz.q: What should you do first to prepare the head for cooking?
quiz.explanation: Singeing removes any remaining hair before washing and further processing.

quiz.q: Which part of the head is considered a delicacy?
quiz.explanation: The brain is often considered a delicacy in many cultures.

quiz.q: Why is chilling the carcass important?
options: A) It firms up the meat and extends shelf life
B) It makes the meat tougher
quiz.explanation: Chilling firms the meat, makes cutting easier, and slows bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What is the ideal chilling temperature for meat?
quiz.explanation: Meat should be chilled to below 4Â°C to prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: If you don't have a refrigerator, what is an alternative method for chilling meat?
options: A) Use ice in a cooler box
quiz.explanation: Packing meat with ice in a cooler box is an effective alternative chilling method.

quiz.q: How long should you ideally chill the carcass?
quiz.explanation: Chilling for 12â24 hours allows rigor mortis to resolve and improves tenderness.

quiz.q: Why is weighing and recording yields important?
options: A) For accurate pricing and business management
quiz.explanation: Weighing yields helps set fair prices and track business performance.

quiz.q: What is the typical dressed carcass weight for a 90 kg live pig?
quiz.explanation: Dressed carcass weight is about 70â75% of live weight, so 63â68 kg.

quiz.q: What should you use to weigh meat?
quiz.explanation: A digital hanging scale or platform scale is accurate for weighing meat.

quiz.q: Why should you record sales?
options: A) To know which cuts sell best
quiz.explanation: Recording sales helps identify popular cuts and plan future production.

quiz.q: What is the first step when splitting the carcass along the spine?
options: A) Start at the tail end
quiz.explanation: Sawing should begin at the tail end and proceed along the spine.

quiz.q: What can happen if you force the saw while splitting?
options: A) The saw may jump and cause injury
quiz.explanation: Forcing the saw can cause it to jump, leading to accidents.

quiz.q: Which primal cut runs along the back from shoulder to ham?
quiz.explanation: The loin is the back muscle running from shoulder to ham.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield percentage of the shoulder?
quiz.explanation: The shoulder typically accounts for about 20% of carcass weight.

quiz.q: What should you do after removing the head?
quiz.explanation: The head should be chilled quickly to prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: Which African dish commonly uses pig head?
quiz.explanation: Pig head is often used in pepper soup in West Africa.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of wiping cut surfaces after sawing?
quiz.explanation: Bone dust can negatively affect appearance and taste.

quiz.q: How many quarters do you get from a carcass?
quiz.explanation: Halving gives two sides, then each side is quartered, resulting in four quarters.

quiz.q: What is a common method for cooling meat without electricity?
quiz.explanation: A zeer pot uses evaporation to cool meat in hot climates.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records for at least a year?
options: A) To compare yields and improve efficiency
quiz.explanation: Long-term records help track performance and make informed decisions.
